summary: Defines and registers two new RTCP Source Description items. One, RtpStreamId, uniquely identifies an RTP stream; the other, RepairedRtpStreamId, says which stream a redundancy stream is repairing. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Each video stream gets a name badge that travels with it. This document creates two kinds of badges: one that says who the stream is, and one that says which stream a backup is helping fix.

questions: how to identify an rtp stream with rtcp sdes
how to identify an rtp stream
subtitle: Two RTCP name tags that tell apart the individual streams inside one RTP session.

tldr.problem: In an RTP session, SSRC values are not guaranteed stable, and CNAME and MSID can appear on more than one stream, so none of them names a single stream. Payload types run out of values when used for this.
tldr.mechanism: RtpStreamId is an RTCP SDES item (also carried in an RTP header extension) that uniquely names one RTP stream. RepairedRtpStreamId lets a redundancy stream point at the stream it repairs.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can match each incoming stream to the right media description, for example when several encodings of one source are sent at once (simulcast). The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8852 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of these two SDES items.

sections.title: Why Streams Need Their Own Identifier
sections.content:
An RTP session often carries several streams, and each is identified at any moment by its synchronization source (SSRC). The RFC points out that the SSRC of a stream is not guaranteed to be stable over its lifetime. Other tags exist, such as CNAMEs and MediaStream Identification (MSID, RFC 8830), but they can appear in more than one stream at a time, so they cannot point at one individual stream.

Some applications give every stream its own payload type (PT). The RFC calls this a semantic overloading of that field, and the field is too small: in moderately complex systems it is possible to run out of values.

The motivating case is simulcast, where different encodings of a single source stream are sent at the same time. The need also covers dependent streams, such as layers of a layered codec sent on separate streams.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a class where several kids have the same first name. You need a number on each shirt so the teacher knows exactly who is who. Streams need that kind of unique tag.

sections.title: RtpStreamId and RepairedRtpStreamId
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new RTCP Source Description (SDES) items. RtpStreamId carries an identifier for an RTP stream. It lets a receiver associate received RTP packets with a media description that has the right format constraints. RepairedRtpStreamId is used in redundancy RTP streams to say which RTP stream is being repaired.

The value in a RepairedRtpStreamId always matches the RtpStreamId of another stream in the same session. If a source stream has RtpStreamId A, any redundancy stream repairing it carries a RepairedRtpStreamId of A. Such a redundancy stream may also have its own RtpStreamId.

This mechanism is limited to one repaired stream per redundancy stream. Schemes where one redundancy stream repairs several streams need a more complex mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: One badge says "I am stream A". A second badge, worn by a helper stream, says "I am here to help stream A".

sections.title: Scope and Allowed Values
sections.content:
Identifier values are scoped by the source identifier (for example the CNAME) and by the media session. When media is multiplexed with BUNDLE (RFC 8843), the values are further scoped by the MID. An RtpStreamId of 1 under two different CNAMEs, or under two different MIDs, refers to two different streams.

Like all SDES items, both identifiers are limited to 255 octets. They may contain only alphanumeric characters, which the RFC spells out as byte values decimal 48 through 57, 65 through 90 and 97 through 122.
sections.plainLanguage: The number 1 on a shirt only means something inside one team. Another team can have its own player number 1.

sections.title: On the Wire: SDES Items and Header Extensions
sections.content:
In RTCP, each item is a one-octet type, a one-octet length and the identifier. RtpStreamId uses item type 12 and RepairedRtpStreamId uses 13. The payload is ASCII and is not null terminated.

RTCP may not be quick enough at stream startup or after a change, and a stream often cannot be processed until it is identified. So the RFC also carries both identifiers in RTP packets, using the RTP header extension for RTCP SDES items (RFC 7941). The element can use either the one-byte or the two-byte header form of RFC 8285.

Header extensions make packets bigger, so implementers should account for the size to avoid MTU problems. The set of extensions in a packet needs to be padded to the next 32-bit boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: The badge can be sent in the slow mail (RTCP) or stapled right onto every package (the RTP header), so the receiver knows right away who it is from.

sections.title: Choosing Identifier Values
sections.content:
In many cases a one-byte identifier is enough to tell streams apart in a session, and implementations are strongly encouraged to use the shortest identifier that fits.

Implementors are warned not to put information derived from potentially user-identifying data, such as a user ID or IP address, in the identifier. To avoid revealing which implementation generated the tags, they are encouraged to use a simple scheme that starts with the ASCII digit 1 and increments by one for each later identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the badge simple: just a small number. Do not write your home address on it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Even though these identifiers are strictly alphanumeric, SDES items can in general carry any string, so they might carry privacy-sensitive information. Following the generation advice above gives non-instance-specific labels, with only minor fingerprinting possibilities in the total number of identifiers used. Implementors are strongly encouraged to encrypt SDES items, in RTCP and in header extensions, to protect privacy against third parties.

An attacker, or a malicious RTP middlebox, that removes or changes these values can severely affect the application. The media might fail to decode or display, or be attributed to the wrong source, such as the wrong speaker. Integrity and source authentication are needed, and RFC 7201 discusses the options for securing RTP sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone swaps the badges, you might think the wrong kid is talking. So the badges should be sealed and checked.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC adds two items to the IANA "RTP SDES Item Types" registry: value 12 for RtpStreamId and value 13 for RepairedRtpStreamId. It also adds two extension URIs to the "RTP SDES Compact Header Extensions" subregistry: urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:rtp-stream-id and a matching URI for the repaired stream identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of badge types gets two new entries so everyone uses the same numbers.
